posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
I am working on the Wiki and am wondering about what we can write about beam ratios. I have experience in reflection H2s and set beam ratio by eye but I am sure we can write something a little better. 

I have heard of people using 4 to 1 for transmission masters to lower noise.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
One caveat to include is that the ratio depends on the film, subject and processing regime.

For PFG-01 film processed with CWC2 and bleached with EDTA I use a 2:1 ratio for my transmission holograms and sometimes post treat them with 1-2% Ascorbic acid to increase contrast.

For reflection H2s using the same film and chemicals I measure light from each source in order to figure the approximate exposure time but use a piece of plain white paper in my plateholder and adjust the ratio until I can *just* see the H1 image from the reference side of the H2 plateholder. That works well where there's high contrast areas in the H1. If the brightness of the projected image is approximately uniform across the H2 preview paper, I'll actually measere both to get a ratio of close to 1:1.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Thank you that helps. I understand that the limit to how bright you can make the object beam is when the bright points of the object start making gratings with other parts of the object. So an object with a specular reflection needs to be dimmer than a perfectly diffuse object. 

Likewise a specular reflection needs to be placed away from the film plane in an H2. to avoid burn in.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Tom, Jeff explain to me once on the correct usage of ratios. Basically I think the idea is because it is a "ratio" always put the large number first. I never knew that. I thought you could put which ever number you wanted first as long as it was explained which one was which.

Mathematically he's right but in all the holographic literature I recall reading, the ratios are as Tom wrote. Ref:Obj. Most don't explain which is which and if you just flip them about all higgeldy piggeldy then you'd never know how much light people were talking about for each beam.

In general the reference light will be greater than the object light, because the ref forms the base signal for your hologram and you usually want the signal to be stronger than the "noise" from the object light. There are some cases where the object light is stronger though and if we stick to the ref:obj usage one never needs to wonder which is which unless the writer religiously specifies his usage each time.

> **MichaelH:** in all the holographic literature I recall reading, the ratios are as Tom wrote. Ref:Obj. Most don't explain which is which ...

Yes, I've observed this too, and it's pretty exasperating if you aren't aware of the unwritten convention.

In the same way that uncommon or hard-to-remenber acronyms should always be spelled out at least once, I would propose that all conscientious holography writers attach a "ref:obj" reminder to their first mention of a beam ratio in an article.

For example - "The Black Cat at Midnight hologram was particularly challenging, with beam ratios exceeding 10000:1 ref:obj".

posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
I've always heard it as reference to object beam ratio, except when I worked at Fermilab on the 15' Bubble Chamber Holography Project. The imperious physicists, who were always re-inventing the wheel, had christened their Beam Balance Ratio with the object first, reference second, and thought I was incorrect with the usual holographic rendering.

I think that the reason why it's reference first is because holographic engineeringese grew out of radio; don't forget that Emmet Leith et al. were working in side-looking radar and got side-tracked into holography. I may be wrong but I think that radio engineers talk about the carrier to signal ratio when describing the modulation of a transmission.

posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md: I always wonder about the ratio which is given for recording laser transmission (H1) holograms. Gives this a sense at all?? In my opinion the problem for this is that only waves of same polarisation interfere. With most objects you get a diffuse reflection and the light is depolarized. So from the entire object light only about a half of the power interferes with the linear polarized reference beam. This is very depended of the object. So how do you measure beam ratios for recording H1 ? For H2s it makes more sense because both beams have same polarisation.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md:
> I have wondered if I should or if I'd get better control over the final brightness in replay.

The effect would be to essentially change the zero set point of your metering system. The fact that most holographers either don't do what you suggest, or do some variation of it, is one of the reasons we get our best results at unique beam ratios. Same thing as whether we account for reflections or not. 

You could record the hologram with a polarizer in front of the object. This makes a brighter, cleaner image for a given beam ratio because the gratings formed by the extra object light are prevented. It means you can decrease the beam ratio, making the hologram even brighter (until the previous signal to noise level is achieved). Of course, this usually isn't very practical unless you have lots of light to use.

posts.author: Ron Michael
posts.content_md:
Colin,

Also to point out that beam ratios may be confusing if not qualified. Most of this discussion is related to as measured at the film plane which takes in all setup issues and the reflectivity of the object and the reference energy density. Some use an average object values while some use the maximum value from the specular highlight. But in split beam holography, the beamspitters, illumination size and loss, and object reflectivity affect setup beam ratios which can be controlled by variable beamsplitters or by a polarizing beamsplitter and half wave plates. So from the setup position, object beams generally are the brigher source. This may be obvious to most holographers but not to a novice. In my pulse work I refer to the setup ratios. Typical for my setup are: 5:70:14 for ref:obj1:obj2. I use two photodiodes meters and a digital storage oscilloscope to measure the actual film ratios which by the way generally are around 1.5:1 Ref:obj when shooting a subject. But additonally the meters are used to measure also the energy density on the subject as well, regarding irradiance safety calculations and film exposure levels.

posts.author: Ron Michael

Ed you are right and of course in other publications it was taken further by incorporating non-linear transfer characteristics of the film. posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
These are all good concepts but for me I only make split beam transmission holograms where the efficiency is not as important as the noise. Noise is the level of fog seen in the image. Then when I make a reflection copy the beam ratio sets the image brightness. Having a more efficient master (H1) only shortens my H2 exposure time. While making the reflection copy the beams remain polarized anyway.

For making bright split beam reflection masters it is crucial to avoid intermodulation from the object. This is the recording of a fringe structure from points on the object acting like additional reference beams. I have always tried to avoid this but I have seen examples recently where a bright secondary hologram was produced but did not dim the intended hologram. Hmm... Perhaps since the secondary fringes are on a different plane the effect is not as bad as calculated...

posts.author: HoloM
posts.content_md: So I still don't understand the proposal of 8:1 or 4:1 ref:obj for transmission masters. I made a test today: I placed a lot of figures on my table and recorded a master hologram with a ratio of 4:1. It was bright and all the figures clearly visible. Then I took away most of the objects, so only one figure was left. Due to fewer light reflecting objects the ratio decreased to about 50: 1 ref:obj. So in the opinion of most books I would have to increase object light to achieve again a ratio of 4:1. But in my opinion, this is not necessary. Because if the figure was bright in the first hologram, it must be bright in the second, too, if I don't change any parameter except removing the other objects. In the first recording only few light comes from one single object to the plate, but this is sufficient to produce a bright hologram of this object. The sum of the reflected light of all objects gives then the ratio of 4:1. If I take away the other figures, there has nothing changed for my object left. So I don't see why I should increase object light for the second recordung. I tried this and the figure was as bright as in the first hologram. I measured the ratio and it was about 50:1. So my opinion is, that the given ratios are very depended on the used objects. Especially if you use a big or small object. So there isn't a chance to compare I think.

posts.author: Tony
posts.content_md:
HoloM-

After you took most of the objects away, the ratio went to 50:1 but the remaining object was just as bright.

But if you now readjusted the ratio back to 4:1, it could have been that much brighter!

Your point is correct, that for given illumination, the light from the object depends on the size and reflectivity of the object.

The point is the film only has a limited dynamic range, and for max brightness, we need to use as much of that range as possible...
